wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.notes: A short, thin finger step off the scramble approach at the 'J Pine' start marks the first real climbing.
A 5.8 squeeze chimney is the lower ridge's first technical test.
A short, straightforward pitch easing off after the chimney.
An insecure layback delivers what one well-documented account calls the lower ridge's overall technical crux; parties have fallen or aided through it.
Simul-climbing begins here: hand jamming, laybacking, and mantling on clean, athletic granite along the ridge crest.
Continued simul-block climbing along the exposed crest.
Sustained low/mid-5th class ridge climbing with excellent position.
More of the same enjoyable ridge-crest climbing.
Continue over towers on the ridge with occasional short downclimbs.
Bomber rock, fun and exposed, typical of the mid-ridge character.
A fantastic 5.5 slab with a crack, a standout pitch just below the Great Gendarme.
Easier ground closing the gap to the base of the Gendarme.
Approach pitches directly below the Gendarme tower.
Final pitch to the Gendarme's base, where the two crux pitches begin.
The Great Gendarme's first pitch: a series of 5.8-5.9 laybacks, underclings, and corners, with a notably strenuous final layback — widely called the route's most demanding pitch.
The Gendarme's infamous 'wide crack' — surprisingly moderate in practice, with bomber fist jams rather than true offwidth technique.
A final 5.7 hand crack closes out the ridge's technical climbing.
Broken, easier terrain trending right back to the crest and on to the true summit.

wa_liberty_crack_free.notes: Identical to the original Liberty Crack P1: a right-facing corner then splitter crack to a bolted belay below the Lithuanian Lip.

The Lithuanian Lip, free: fun 5.11- corner climbing leads to a scrunchy, powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip; lock in, high-step to the lip, and stick 5.12- moves to a small stance below the old bolt ladder. This is the pitch Brooke Sandahl first led on gear in 1991.

The modern free variation (Schaefer/Lee/Herrington/Hadley, 2016-17) that avoids the crumbling bolt ladder: move right, clip a higher bolt, cross sloping ledges, and mantel through cruxy foot moves past four protection bolts before rejoining the original line.
A thin crux move gains a small roof before the pitch rejoins the original Liberty Crack line below easier ground.
Jam a crack that hardens from 5.8 to 5.10, same as the original route's corresponding pitch, to a bolted belay.
A relatively relaxed corner pitch to another bolted belay.
Mostly easy stemming to a brief crux surmounting a big block past a single shiny bolt.
Steep moves off the belay to a ramp/corner with a long-runner bolt and an overlap move to a small seat.
Fun quartz features and 5.6 chimneys lead to a triangular ledge with a finger-crack gear anchor.
A long, excellent corner-and-slab pitch with airy East Face exposure, ending at a large tree belay.
Easy terrain leads to sandy ledges below the summit shoulder.
Easy simul-climbing/scrambling gains the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder, the top of the shared two-rappel descent into Beckey Gully.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: Climbs the right edge of the East Face on horizontal breaks and cracks to a belay near a yellow lichen patch by a pine tree.
Crimp right then traverse left on a flake through a bolted section that follows the historic aid pendulum's line.
A left-facing quartz corner with a hard right-stemming sequence near two bolts.
Chimney/offwidth climbing for about 40 ft to a small alcove below the red 'Baer Ceiling,' an original aid pitch.
A ramp into a shallow corner with cruxy face moves protected by a fixed pin and copperheads; a mantle and slab move reach the belay. A sneaky, often-underrated crux.
A thin, piton-protected crack passes three stacked 'Cascade Ceilings' via a mantle move.
A technical rightward traverse into a shallow corner above a pine tree, with a reach-dependent boulder-problem section -- the original crux before the route's belays were repositioned.
Technical, classic granite stemming and jamming up an exposed corner beneath the 'Well Hung Ceiling' -- the route's overall crux pitch, matching its full free grade.
Short pitch moving the belay left onto M&M Ledge, shared with Liberty Crack and Thin Red Line.
Chimney and blocky corner climbing past red roofs to the base of a splitter wide crack; an alternate left-trending ramp also exists.
A nice splitter 2-3 inch crack leads to a clean slab and bolted anchor beneath the Hercan Roofs.
A slab traverse up and right gains the ridge crest, followed by 3rd-class scrambling to the summit.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Start low in the moat below the buttress. Climb clean, well-protected granite slabs to a ledge, then follow it left to a good belay. If the cracks straight above the start are wet, the slab to their right is the alternative.

Take the gully on the left, not the steep option straight up. After about 50 ft, at a large ledge, turn right up a steep face of big jugs on solid rock with no protection. Trend up and right to the next major crack or gully for the anchor.

Runout. Head up and left, then break right into the main corner system. A knifeblade piton protects the step right onto a slab. Friable, discontinuous corners lead to an indistinct ledge with a fixed #1 knifeblade at the belay. The big open-book corner above is steep, mossy and loose; do not take it.

Head up and right. Avoid the obvious open-book corner and make a hard-to-spot step up and right onto the slab. A gentle rising traverse right includes about 25 ft of 5.10 face climbing on excellent rock. It ends at a stance by some flakes, where you belay.

Up delicate flakes, then step right into a good crack as soon as possible. Well-protected crack climbing leads past a roof crux. Where the cracks fork, take the right one past a couple of vegetated moves to a cramped belay built around a good #3 cam placement.

Continue up the crack to a rubble-covered ledge. A short, technical finger crack reaches an obvious ledge system. Traverse it right all the way to the huge gully, then run the rope up the rib beside the gully to a heather ledge belay.
Move into the huge gully, which is lined with solid, water-polished rock rather than rubble. Stem up it for a full rope length.
Continue up the polished gully to a saddle on the ridge crest. Scramble gravel and heather to an anchor at the base of the steeper wall above.
Climb compact rock up and right past gravel-covered ledges to an anchor. There is essentially no protection on this pitch.
Up the ridge crest. From here the good gneiss gives way to the compact, shattered rock typical of the Pickets. Gear is sparse.
Simul-climb the ridge to the notch below the west summit, on shattered rock with limited protection. Take care not to knock rock onto a partner below.
4th-class scrambling from the notch up to the west summit of Whatcom Peak.

co_childhood_s_end.notes: Begin a few metres right of the large boulder at the foot of the buttress. A low-angle crack with a tree in it crosses the face to a two-bolt station below a short chimney holding a 6-10 inch crack.
Climb the chimney (a #4 Camalot low, or a #2 higher), then the slab above past five bolts.

Step right to a crack, climb it about 20 ft, then step left onto a slab with three bolts. A 5.11 variation steps sharply left past two bolts into a water groove and past one more bolt before rejoining the slab.
Clip a bolt out left, go around the corner, and climb the slab past two bolts. The last stretch to the anchor is run out.
Clip the first bolt, climb right to the arete and past a couple of bolts, then make a long reach up and left to a ledge with a two-bolt anchor. Belaying here reduces rope drag.
Climb about 20 ft to the first bolt, traverse right about 15 ft to a hard-to-see bolt, and continue right over a ridge. The zig-zag line causes drag even with long draws.

The crux. Climb up to a finger crack and an undercling and clip a bolt, then move around onto the steep right side, underclinging past about 11 bolts before going straight up. It aids easily, and some think the hard section is best aided.
Long, sustained climbing past nine or ten bolts, with a hard move left into a groove worn by water, then the ground eases.
Slabs about 30 m up and left to a single bolt roughly 20 ft out left of the direct line, then up and right about 20 m to a new two-bolt anchor. Can be simul-climbed.
Continue up slab climbing past one bolt to a new two-bolt anchor.
No bolts and no gear. Ends at a large tree or the top of the cliff. Loose or damp lichen and snapping crystals demand focus.

wa_beyond_redlining.notes: Climbs the dark gray face above the two largest boulders at the tower's base, with multiple cruxes leading to a roof breached on the right side.
Navigate a bulge, ascend a rib, and traverse a steep slab; watch for loose rock in the approach gully below.
A more serious pitch than the grade suggests: polished rock, sparse bolts, and few positive holds on a left-trending ramp.
Low-angle terrain traversing above a large ledge to the belay.
Three fun cruxes lead to a featured, vertical finish on a large ledge system.
A steep face with a tricky bulge at an orange band; extend draws to manage rope drag. An unfinished, harder direct variant exists here but is not recommended as bolted.
A fun slab with easy runout, then steep athletic moves and a punchy crux at a bulge.
A looming, very airy headwall with a wild corner past a couple of roofs.
Steeper than it looks: steep jugs, side-pulls, and jams on an overhanging face.
A golden, featured slab with a crux bulge, then an arête past a curious 'Mouth' feature.
A tricky boulder problem at the top of the pillar — the route's final and hardest crux — just below the summit shared with Mile High Club.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Starts up a crack behind a short chimney block that becomes a left-facing corner, then works around a roof to the left; launched from a pedestal belay in the gully between Cathedral and 'The Monk'.
Navigate a steep chockstone — climbing behind and over it gives a bombproof terrain belay — then exit right into juggy cracks.
Stem and jam excellent twin finger cracks, mantle out of the corner system, step right to a short wide crack, then back onto twin finger cracks.
Follows a quartz dike with a leftward traverse to the belay; discontinuous, juggy climbing with limited protection, so place gear smartly to manage rope drag.
Climb a right-facing corner to a cruxy mantle move, then ramble up ledges to a chimney on the right.
A finger crack leads to an open book corner, then the climbing eases into 3rd-4th class terrain toward the headwall.
Easy, discontinuous terrain approaching the base of the headwall; many parties simul-climb this section to save time before the crux above.
A tricky move down low earns a solid medium cam before an obvious double-crack system up the start of the headwall; commonly linked with P9 into a single 55m 5.10a pitch.

Step rightward and choose between a wide crack or the harder, equally splitter finger crack further right (the more popular option); linked with P8 this becomes a sustained 55m 5.10a pitch and the technical crux of the route.
Two short, fun hand-crack steps separated by a ledge lead to 3rd class scrambling and the true summit.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.anchor: Gear, then unroped 3rd class to the summit
